appraisal_events.evidence: Bloch praises Saint-Loup as « extrêmement bien élevé » « sans se rendre compte, parce qu’il était lui-même très mal élevé, combien ses paroles déplaisaient »; his climactic revelation about Sir Rufus Israël falls flat because « aux yeux du milieu Guermantes » Israël is « un étranger parvenu, toléré par le monde, et de l’amitié de qui on n’eût pas eu l’idée de s’enorgueillir »; he speaks with « cet accent d’enthousiasme qu’on n’apporte qu’aux convictions qu’on ne s’est pas formées soi-même ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator systematically undercuts Bloch: his lecture on good breeding exposes his own bad breeding, his attempted prestige coup misreads the social currency of the room, and his borrowed enthusiasm is diagnosed as second-hand. The intended self-elevation is turned into a public misfire that the assembled company finds displeasing or unintelligible.

appraisal_events.evidence: « C’est quelqu’un de très mal [...] De très, très mal, reprit-elle en mettant trois t à très », said « avec l’accent vertueux des Guermantes même les plus dépravés »; her frowning severity toward « l’horrible capitaine » culminates in her pronouncing « avec une emphase ironique » the name « le Prince de Borodino », « en femme pour qui l’Empire ne compte pas ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Villeparisis condemns Borodino morally (as accomplice of an « liaison infâme ») and socially, mocking his Napoleonic title from a legitimist vantage. The narrator ironizes her virtue by attributing it to a caste whose most depraved members share the same tone, so Borodino's loss registers as caste-coded contempt rather than narrator-endorsed judgment.

status_effects.explanation: Bloch is clearly diminished: the narrator shows his discourse on breeding refuting itself, his manners offending, and his convictions being borrowed.
His bid for standing through acquaintance with Sir Rufus Israël fails in this room, where such a connection carries no prestige and his story remains merely incomprehensible.
He is branded « de très, très mal », suspected of orgies, and has his imperial title pronounced with derision by the Guermantes voice, which locally lowers him in that milieu.

The narrator lightly lowers her in the act of her own moralizing: the virtuous accent is that of « des Guermantes même les plus dépravés », and her charm closes on a « clignement d’œil mécanique de connivence vague ».

Within the anecdote used to diminish Bloch, Saint-Loup's breeding is credited by both Bloch and the narratorial frame — he stays « simple », unembarrassed, and needs not tremble before the Israël name — which outweighs the passing « mauvais chien » and the family's talk of his liaison.

ambiguities: Villeparisis's condemnation of Borodino is doubly framed: the family's hostility is reported as real, but the narrator's phrase « l’accent vertueux des Guermantes même les plus dépravés » withholds endorsement, so the event is read here as ironized caste contempt rather than a narrator-backed moral verdict.

Sir Rufus Israël is evaluated in two incompatible registers at once (« un personnage presque royal » for the Blochs, « un étranger parvenu » for the Guermantes milieu); the passage is read here as staging Bloch's misjudgment rather than as a status movement for Israël himself, who is absent and mention-only.
